pseudonyms: M. C. (initials, Little Arthur's History of England, 1835)
nationality_or_literary_tradition: British - a Romantic-period writer of travel journals, art history, scientific observation and school books, born in Cumberland into a Scottish naval family and at home in the Edinburgh publishing world, the London review circles, the Geological Society and the Royal Academy.
literary_identity: Travel writer and children's author, with art history, translation and geological observation on either side: the first woman to publish an article in the Transactions of the Geological Society, and the author of the most durable school history of the mid-nineteenth century. Her proper form is the journal of residence - daily observation, measured, documented and drawn by her own hand - and the instructed child's book built upon it.
biography: Maria Dundas was born at Papcastle, near Cockermouth, Cumberland, on 19 July 1785, eldest child of George Dundas (1756-1814), a Royal Navy officer who rose to rear-admiral. She met Samuel Rogers and Thomas Campbell at her uncle Sir David Dundas's Richmond house. In December 1808 she sailed with her father to Bombay; on 9 December 1809 she married a fellow passenger, Captain Thomas Graham, R.N., and travelled in India, returning to England in June 1811. Her Journal of a Residence in India appeared in 1812, Letters on India in 1814 and her translation of Rocca's Memoirs of the War of the French in Spain in 1815-16. Italy in 1819 yielded Three Months Passed in the Mountains East of Rome and the Memoirs of the Life of Nicholas Poussin, both of 1820. Sailing for the Pacific in HMS Doris in 1821, she was widowed off Cape Horn in April 1822 and passed the next year at Valparaiso, where she observed the great earthquake of November 1822; her account of the raised seabed, printed in the Transactions of the Geological Society in 1824, was the first article by a woman in that series, entered Lyell's Principles of Geology in 1830, was ridiculed by Greenough and vindicated by Darwin's Chilean evidence. Her Chile and Brazil journals appeared in 1824, and after teaching the young Donna Maria da Gloria at Rio she reached England in 1825. The Voyage of the H.M.S. Blonde to the Sandwich Islands, compiled from official papers and the Bloxams' journals, came in 1826; on 20 February 1827 she married the painter Augustus Wall Callcott, R.A., and her A Short History of Spain followed in 1828. A ruptured blood vessel in 1831 confined her to the desk: Giotto's chapel at Padua and Little Arthur's History of England in 1835, the Histoire de France du petit Louis in 1836, Essays towards the History of Painting in 1836-38, The Little Bracken-Burners in 1841 and A Scripture Herbal in 1842. Callcott was knighted in 1837 and she became Lady Callcott; she died at the Kensington Gravel Pits and lies in Kensal Green Cemetery.
literary_profile: Her work divides into four streams. The travel journals: Journal of a Residence in India (1812), Letters on India, with Etchings and a Map (1814), Three Months Passed in the Mountains East of Rome (1820), Journal of a Residence in Chile during the year 1822 and a Voyage from Chile to Brazil in 1823 (1824), Journal of a Voyage to Brazil (1824), and the compiled Voyage of the H.M.S. Blonde to the Sandwich Islands (1826). Art history and translation: Rocca's Memoirs of the War of the French in Spain (1815-16), Memoirs of the Life of Nicholas Poussin (1820), the Description of the Chapel of the Annunziata dell'Arena, or Giotto's Chapel in Padua (1835), and Essays towards the History of Painting (1836-38). Books for children and the nursery: Little Arthur's History of England (1835), its French pendant Histoire de France du petit Louis (1836), and The Little Bracken-Burners with Little Mary's Four Saturdays (1841). Devotional natural history: A Scripture Herbal (1842). She etched plates for her own books, and her geological letters form a separate printed body.
stylistic_characteristics: A plain, exact and deliberately unadorned prose of observation, strong in measurement, level, date and named informant, and modest about itself. She attributes knowledge readily - to her father's naval and Orientalist books, to interpreters, to the Bloxams' journals - and yet keeps a distinct first-person presence. Botanical and geological detail is given in the technical language of her authorities, drawn as well as written, her etchings and sketches carrying part of the argument. Controversy sharpens her: her reply to Greenough is combative and closely quoted. In Little Arthur the manner changes to the catechetical and conversational, an uncle telling English chronology to a child reader, with moral and patriotic point made plainly and the sentences shortened for the nursery.
intellectual_concerns: The authority of the eyewitness against the authority of sex and office; the uplift of coasts, the record of earthquakes and the reading of the earth's changes; the instruction of children as the making of citizens, and patriotic history taught in the nursery; the religious content of natural history, pursued in A Scripture Herbal; the appreciation and classification of painting, from Poussin to Giotto and the Paduan frescoes; the duties of a European in India, Chile and the court of Brazil, and the value of accurate account of native peoples, Parsi worship and Sanskrit learning; the education of princesses and the political uses of tutoring.
historical_significance: She was among the most successful women travel writers of the Romantic generation and the chief English eyewitness of the 1822 Chilean earthquakes: her letter to Henry Warburton, printed in the Transactions of the Geological Society in 1824, is the first article by a woman in that series, and her observation of coastal elevation passed into Lyell's Principles of Geology (1830), was mocked by Greenough and later supported by Darwin's evidence. Her Poussin memoir of 1820 gave English readers their first sustained life of the painter; her journals remain primary authority on Chilean independence and on the Brazilian court of Pedro I; the Blonde volume is a chief source for that voyage. Little Arthur's History of England remained a standard child's history for three quarters of a century, and Chile honours her as an early friend of its nationhood.
major_influences: Carsten Niebuhr's accounts of Indian antiquity
Charles Wilkins and Henry Thomas Colebrooke
Nicolas Poussin and the Italian primitives
Henry Warburton and the Geological Society of London
biographical_uncertainty: The years are firm (born 19 July 1785; died 1842), but the day of death is given as 28 November 1842 by the Dictionary of National Biography and as 21 November 1842 by most modern accounts; her burial in Kensal Green Cemetery is documented. The birthplace is given by the Dictionary of National Biography and by the British Travel Writing project as Papcastle near Cockermouth, Cumberland, though Wikipedia words it as 'near Cockermouth', and no parish register has been checked here. The batch brief assigns her The History of Little Henry and his Bearer (1814): that tale is attributed in the Dictionary of National Biography, in the standard children's-literature scholarship (M. N. Cutt), in library catalogues and in the Hockliffe Collection to Mary Martha Sherwood, who composed it anonymously in India; no contemporary impression connects it with Maria Graham, whose own books for children begin with Little Arthur in 1835, and the attribution is therefore not accepted in this record. Her Brazilian teaching service is variously dated: the Dictionary of National Biography has her instructress to Donna Maria from 22 November 1822 to January 1823, while later accounts place the court engagement after her 1824 return to Rio, and her unpublished 'Memoir of the Life of Don Pedro' survives only in manuscript. The share of the Blonde volume that is her own composition, the volume having been made from official papers and the journals of the chaplain R. Rowland Bloxam and the naturalist Andrew Bloxam, is open to judgement.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Scottish and British - a Romantic-period political economist, statistician and reviewer: an Edinburgh-trained Ricardian who made his career in London, and the genre-defining writer of the expository treatise, the review article and the statistical dictionary.
literary_identity: A publicist and systematiser of political economy rather than an original theorist - the man who made Ricardo a curriculum. His proper forms are the expository treatise, the review article, the pamphlet addressed to a parliamentary committee, and the statistical dictionary built from consular returns; his most lasting single performance is the Introductory Discourse prefixed to Adam Smith, where a science is given a history, a pedigree and a canon of texts.
biography: John Ramsay McCulloch was born at Whithorn, Wigtownshire, on 1 March 1789, eldest son of Edward McCulloch, laird of Auchengool in the stewartry of Kirkcudbright, and Sarah Laing. His father died while he was a child and his grandfather taught him first; after his mother's remarriage he went to school at Kinross, then attended Edinburgh University without taking a degree, sitting with Sir John Leslie, who became his friend, and with Thomas Brown, from whom he learned to distrust metaphysics. He entered a writer to the signet's office and soon left it in disgust. His Essay on a Reduction of the Interest of the National Debt (1816) drew Ricardo's correspondence, and his Edinburgh Review essay on Ricardo's Principles of 1818 began twenty years of periodical writing, seventy-six articles in all by 1837. He helped to found The Scotsman in 1817, edited it from 1818 to 1820 and wrote its economic copy for a decade. In 1824 he delivered the Ricardo Memorial Lectures in London, which became A Discourse on the Rise, Progress, Peculiar Objects, and Importance of Political Economy (1824), the Britannica article on Political Economy, and The Principles of Political Economy with a Sketch of the Rise and Progress of the Science (1825), the standard textbook until Mill's treatise of 1848. The Essay on the Circumstances which Determine the Rate of Wages (1826) gave the English-speaking world the wages-fund doctrine, and his edition of Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations with an Introductory Discourse appeared in 1828, the year he took the unendowed chair of political economy at the new University of London. Principles, Practice and History of Commerce (1831) and his Dictionary of Commerce and Commercial Navigation (1832) were followed by the Descriptive and Statistical Account of the British Empire (1837), the geographical dictionary of 1841, the Treatise on Taxation and the Funding System (1845), The Literature of Political Economy (1845), his edition of Ricardo's Works (1846) and the Political Economy Club's collections of scarce tracts (1856-59). Comptroller of the Stationery Office from 1838, he died there on 11 November 1864 and lies in Brompton Cemetery.
literary_profile: His work is systematic rather than imaginative, and divides into four bodies. Treatise and textbook: A Discourse on the Rise, Progress, Peculiar Objects, and Importance of Political Economy (1824) and The Principles of Political Economy, with a Sketch of the Rise and Progress of the Science (1825; enlarged editions 1830, 1843, 1849), with the applied studies An Essay on the Circumstances which Determine the Rate of Wages (1826), the Principles, Practice and History of Commerce (1831) and the treatises on Taxation and the Funding System (1845) and on Succession to Property Vacant by Death (1848). Reference and statistics: the Dictionary, Practical, Theoretical and Historical, of Commerce and Commercial Navigation (1832), the Descriptive and Statistical Account of the British Empire (1837) and the geographical dictionary of 1841. Editing and bibliography: Smith's Wealth of Nations (1828), Ricardo's Works (1846), The Literature of Political Economy (1845) and the tract collections edited for the Political Economy Club and for Lord Overstone (1856-59). Periodical prose: seventy-six Edinburgh Review articles (1818-37) and a decade of economic leading in The Scotsman.
stylistic_characteristics: Bald, emphatic and expository: a prose of definition, enumeration and example, written to be taught from. He repeats himself across book, review and pamphlet until a doctrine becomes a commonplace, and his habitual move is to dispute an opponent's terms rather than his facts. Abstractions are handled concretely - the cask of new wine that gains five pounds in the cellar carries the whole question of profit - and his tables of prices, rents, colonies and population are themselves the evidence. Caricature caught the manner with the accent: Carlyle's McGroudy, Peacock's MacFungus, Christopher North's Stot and the Mordecai Mullion parody of 1826 all satirise a dogmatic, repetitive, plain-spoken Scot.
intellectual_concerns: The labour theory of value and the impossibility of an invariable measure of value; rent and the corn laws; the wages-fund and the condition of the labouring classes; profit, interest and whether time can of itself produce value; taxation, the funding system and the national debt; free trade, colonization and emigration; the statistical knowledge of a commercial state as the ground of legislation; the history, literature and right boundaries of political economy as a science; and the diffusion of economic orthodoxy by textbook, review, professorial chair and discussion class.
historical_significance: He was the leader of the Ricardian school after 1823 and the man who turned it into a teachable public doctrine: his Principles was the orthodoxy that Mill superseded, was translated into French, German and Italian, and made him the most quoted and most abused of economists in his own generation. His editions of Smith and of Ricardo fixed the canon of classical political economy, and their prefaces, with The Literature of Political Economy, founded the history and bibliography of the subject. The Dictionary of Commerce and the Statistical Account of the British Empire set the model of the official factual compendium, and his appointment in 1828 made him the first professor of political economy in the University of London.
biographical_uncertainty: The dates are firm and agreed (born 1 March 1789, died 11 November 1864). The birthplace is given as Whithorn, Wigtownshire, by the Dictionary of National Biography and repeated by modern encyclopedias and by Wikipedia, but the family's standing is reported differently: the Dictionary of National Biography calls his father laird of Auchengool, while social-science encyclopedias describe a small landowner who lost his fortune, so the economics of McCulloch's childhood cannot be stated precisely. The end of his University College professorship is disputed: the Dictionary of National Biography and the Macmillan Encyclopedia of Economic History say he resigned the unendowed chair in 1832, while the History of Economic Thought archive has him holding it until 1837. He is sometimes described as an editor of the Edinburgh Review; the succession from Francis Jeffrey in October 1829 belongs to MacVey Napier, and his relation to the Review should be stated as contributor and its principal writer on political economy. His Treatise on Taxation and the Funding System is dated 1845 by the Dictionary of National Biography and by first-edition imprints, but appears under 1863 in some modern lists, presumably a later issue. The surname is printed both McCulloch and M'Culloch, and the count of seventy-six Review articles is the Dictionary of National Biography's estimate rather than a census.
